chunks: Design a LiPo charge/discharge circuit. The question: Design a circuit to charge/discharge a LiPo.
Designing a LiPo charge and discharge circuit means choosing the blocks that sit between a power source and your device. A charger chip fills the battery safely.
A protection chip guards it. A voltage regulator turns the battery's changing voltage into the steady voltage your electronics need.
Start by deciding what you need, then pick each block.
Think of the water system of a house with a storage tank. A pump fills the tank at a safe rate (the charger).
A safety valve opens if pressure goes too high or the tank runs dry (the protection chip).
A pressure regulator before the tap gives a steady flow, no matter how full the tank is (the voltage regulator).
Where this picture breaks down: a battery's output voltage sinks as it empties, and the regulator has to cope with that.
The system is two power paths around the battery: the charge path (USB to charger to protected cell) and the discharge path (cell to regulator to load).
The power-path charger also lets USB feed the system directly.
The NTC on the cell feeds the charger's temperature input (it can also be shared with the gauge); the gauge reports to the MCU over I²C.
Requirements: the numbers that decide the design, such as battery size, input source, output voltage and load current.
Charger IC: a chip that runs the charging routine ("Why charging and monitoring ICs matter").
Protection IC: a chip with switches that guard against overvoltage, undervoltage, overcurrent and shorts.
Regulator (LDO or buck-boost): a circuit that makes a steady output voltage from the battery's 3. 0 to 4. 2 volts range.
An LDO can only step the voltage down; a buck-boost can step it down or up.
Power path: a charger feature that lets the device run from the input while it also charges the battery.
